The paper presents these as things that were partly undone ('so we restored C's semantics of switch and break'), and does not credit pattern matching, tagged unions, polymorphism or exceptions to ML by name; hence weak and partly. Human to decide.

v2_quote_check.comment: Abstract, first two sentences; the source sentence continues ', while retaining C's syntax and semantics.'

notes: The PDF gave no extractable text, so the HTML version of the same paper on usenix.org was read through the fetch tool (excerpts limited to about 125 characters; the ML quote was returned in two pieces and joined). Off-map: Popcorn, the authors' earlier C-like language ('Cyclone is a reworking of Popcorn with two agendas') and Typed Assembly Language. Java, ML, Modula-3 and Lisp appear in the introduction only as examples of safe languages; C++ and Haskell are not named. The implementation-language route is ML -> Popcorn, not ML -> Cyclone.

named.quote: It was created in 2011 by Neo4j engineers as an SQL-equivalent language for graph databases.
named.what: role model: a declarative query language for graphs as SQL is for tables; shared keywords
named.reason: No better quote exists on the page. It says Cypher was created as an SQL equivalent, which implies modeling, but every other sentence is a comparison ('Similar to SQL, Cypher lets users focus on what to retrieve', 'Cypher and SQL are similar in many ways.'). None says a feature was taken from SQL, so the verdict should be partly rather than supported, and the kind is closer to design than syntax. A human may want a source that states the borrowing (e.g. the openCypher or Neo4j history material).

v2_quote_check.comment: Exact. The sentence about shared keywords (WHERE, ORDER BY) mentioned in the v2 note was not among the sentences returned this time; the page may have been reworded.

notes: The page names no language other than SQL in connection with Cypher's design (no SPARQL, Python, Haskell or GQL in the sentences returned). The page also lists differences: 'SQL queries begin with what a user wants to return, whereas Cypher queries end with the return clause.'
